Author: @TJM-2023
Content:
I've been preparing for a 9950x3D build, because you said Intel's new chip sucks; but AMD is a huge mess for builders who don't have a PHD in computer science.
#1: AM5 cannot handle high-speed RAM. After 6000MT/s, you have to cut the clock in half.
#2: Even if you get AM5 RAM to work, you would have another big struggle if you wanted 4 sticks. Heck, try to even find 4x32 sticks that don't have a CL of 40 or more!!!!
#3: AM5 has a lot of ridiculous settings that need to be set or the system may not run well. These are really obscure things that almost nobody would know about.

Intel: You can use whatever RAM you want in any way you want (well, that's the way it feels compared to the EXTREMELY constrained EXPO shitstorm.
Intel: There's no weird settings you have to adjust. It just works.

Anyway, you stated over and over and over again that AMD was far superior to INTEL; but that's just untrue. Intel is easy to deal with, AMD is a crazy mess of configuration.

Author: @LordofWeebs
Content:
How is the 40 super series a bad product line? Everything else makes sense but tell us how the 4070 Super with it's straight up 14% more power compared to the base 4070, the 4070Ti Super with its 10% more power compared to the 4070Ti and the 4 Gigs of extra VRAM, all of that and being the same price as the base variants make these bad products? For those who already own the non Super variants, sure its not much of a reason to upgrade after a few months but is that the audience which the Super series usually targets? I don't think so. It's to attract a new customer base with the mid generation refresh. 

Granted the 4080 Super was literally just a 2% increase over the 4080 with the 200 dollar drop in price and it would have made more sense just to drop the price of the base 4080 as opposed to introducing a whole new product

But considering the 4070 Super and 4070 Ti Super, how does this overall make the Super series a worst list worthy product? I don't think you have many convinced with this one

But I am genuinely curious, if despite all this you still think the Super series a bad product, then what in your opinion should the 40 super series been to classify it as a good product?

Author: @choppergirl
Content:
Probably the biggest disappointment was the whole 99xx AMD series of chips.  We were expecting a major leap, and got crumbs.   And the 9950x3D... if it indeed has just a single Vcache... what a flop!   All you had to do was put two Vcache's on it to keep it symetrical and make it a beast!

If it's only got a single Vcache, and two... one for each core die, I don't want it. And neither should you. No more unbalanced lopsided chips. I avoided them the first time around and bought a 7950x, and I don't plan on falling for them the second time around... operating systems just do not know how to deal with these lopsided Ryzen 3D chips or Intel Performace Core / Efficience Core chips, and you can be sure older operating systems (like running inside a VM) won't have a clue how to properly schedule on them Slash Avoid buying any chip at all that is not symmetrical throughout at all costs. The industry is already churning out enough garbage as it is. We as consumers don't need to encourage them further.   

A lot of us plan on using Windows 10 as long as we can hold out, and you can be sure it's not going to know how to efficiently schedule on one of these chips.  It can't even do a good job on my 7950x symetrical 16 core chip... you know it's going to fail miserably on a 3D chip or an Intel Performance Efficiciency Core chip.

Author: @WhiteG60
Content:
I think the 7600XT was an OK GPU, because at launch, remember, the driver based framegen was only supposed to be introduced in 7000 series cards. So even if the 6600 was a better value, you were losing out on power consumption and you weren't going to get the advanced features. Once AMD was heckled into letting 6000 series do the FMF, the 'advantage' of the 7600 disappeared. 

The other thing that wasn't talked about was that while the 7800XT had 60 compute units vs the. 6800XT having 72, and the 7800XT being faster and using less power, even if only 5-7% faster. They really should have pushed all the cards down one tier naming wise. 7800XT should have been 7800, 7800 (which doesn't exist) should have been a 7700XT, 7700XT should have been a 7700, etc. If the 7600 had been called a 7500XT for $249, it would have been killer. The cards were good, the naming/marketing were bad. There was room to have something between the 7800XT and the 7900XT, which they did with the GRE, but that's a stupid name. They should have called it a 7900 and left it at that.

Author: @rars0n
Content:
I think it's worth pointing out that Apple ditched Intel after Skylake in large part due to its failure to do proper validation. This was something that I had heard about changing within the company sometime around 2012, at least according to the anecdotes from alleged Intel employees. Skylake particularly stands out to me because I was working in third-party repair at the time, and we had also sold Skylake-based OEM machines to some customers (against my wishes, as I was already aware of its buggy reputation and didn't want to sell customers potentially problematic machines). In one instance, a customer bought 3 Skylake-based Dell desktops for their business and almost immediately 2 of them began to have various issues, with both of them eventually needing to be replaced under warranty. While Skylake was seemingly fine for a lot of builders, I saw _WAY_ more issues with customer OEM machines than any previous generation of Intel processors, and even Kaby Lake seemed vastly improved. IMO, Skylake was a dud. This was around the same time that Intel was pushing Optane quite hard, another product that was seemingly broken at launch.

I have been a fan of AMD since the K6, my budget alternative to the Pentium-based machine that I wanted to build, but even I can recognize the value of a healthy, thriving Intel. The company seems to be continuing down the path of destruction that it started taking over a decade ago. I was really hopeful when Pat took the reigns because it felt like he was exactly the kind of guy they needed in charge, just like AMD needed Lisa. I found it a bit odd that they continued their deceptive marketing tactics, as they were something I figured Pat would put an end to. Overall, I think he was a positive for the company and I suspect his firing is emblematic of the problems that lie deep within the company.

I'm not married to x86 but I think it gets maligned more than it deserves, and I'm not entirely sold on the scaling of ARM. I'd like to see continued competition among CPU architectures though, and I worry that with Intel faltering so hard, x86 might not be long for this world. AMD is certainly picking up the slack, but the market will be done no favors if AMD simply replaces Intel as the CPU giant. I also think the GPU market desperately needs Intel's competition in order to invigorate a stagnating market. Battlemage is quite an impressive product, and at my favorite GPU price point of $300 (I have been buying $300 GPUs since the late 90's). I haven't rushed out to buy one, but I admit it's a little bit tempting to combine an AMD CPU with a discrete Intel GPU just for the sheer oddity of such a combination. Still, it's a sad state of affairs when the only compelling GPU product at $300 is something from Intel. Hopefully that changes with the new GPU releases this year.

Author: @Ryzard
Content:
I just built in the Corsair 6500x for a friend (A Corsair loyalist)
My biggest gripe by FAR is the lack of a manual.
Not only is there not one, the online documentation is INSANELY vague and frustrating to move through, plus it can have load time.
I've built ~12-15 PCs so far over the last few years, and what I've come to know is that manuals are your friends - the very best friends. My friends get exhasperated from how often I ask to be handed one in the middle of a troubleshoot.

What I DO NOT WANT is to have to set down my screwdriver, screw, and flashlight/phone to use said flashlight/phone to try to google a manual - or when that just DOES NOT REALLY EXIST, google a build video, and try to find a 2 second span where the screw I'm trying to look for is shown.

Corsair pisses me off, because (As this was a corsair loyalist) we of course used a corsair PSU, AIO, etc.
NONE OF WHICH HAD MANUALS. Annoyingly, the Motherboard (ASUS) also did not have a manual in the box - which meant I was regularly flipping  between my phone's browser, a downloaded pdf, and several other tabs while trying to line up screws.

The manual cannot cost more than a couple cents to add to a box, but it makes the build experience soooo much smoother and simpler.
At the very least, as Steve said, I wish that the documentation online was in one place and easily browsed...

Other notes - 
*- The glass door (front) panel to this case was either wonky, or had a stripped screw, which made it impossible to remove.*
Building when rotating the case requires clearing the table and figuring out bracing for a heavy glass panel is a pain.
No real notes there, it just sucks, and it couldn't rest on its back without things for the door to lay against, since it didn't have the range of motion to lay on the table, and thus we'd have the glass panel just precariously placing all its weight on a tiny hinge which seems like begging for it to shatter.

*- For the love of god, do not use the SF1000 in this case.*
(You may consider that common sense, but it was the only available 1000w platinum psu that was CORSAIR around black friday near us.)
It does the one thing no sff psu I've used has done, and actually had shorter cables.
That's lovely when you are using an SFF case, but fitting them into this case and reaching the mobo and GPU were painful (literally, my fingers scraped to hell) and used none of the proper routing channels.

*- Also, while I'm sure there's a drawback, or they are impossible to get extras for, the 2-turn (iirc) screws were, surprisingly, one of my FAVORITE parts of this build.*
I hate screwing in fans - you're always fighting potentially stripping screw heads, half the time the screws never want to go in without sliding sideways, etc.
These screws were FANTASTIC, stupidly easy and slid right into place. Sucks that corsair almost certainly copyrighted them though, as I'd love to have them in more builds without paying $100+ over what is reasonable for parts.

Author: @ryanpaaz
Content: I hope intel gets their train back on the tracks.  Like many of you, I didn't like when Intel was high on the hog and clearly in the lead and taking advantage of the position.  I"m also not exactly happy they're having fundamental struggles the way they are.  I'd like us to go back to when AMD and Intel would trade top spot when each released a new product.  It kept the industry as a whole moving forward, and also meant that the pricing was favorable to consumers, especially if you were buying 'last years' tech at closeout.  That said, I think we'd all like them to return to a spot of stability, and perhaps (wishful thinking) see them give Nvidia a run for their money on the GPU side.   With the way the industry is going with modular designs, hopefully this means they can scale up and down a product stack without needing to reinvent the wheel each time.

Author: @Xyler94
Content:
The funny thing about the Asus warranty thing, I did send a non-functional 3080ti to Asus under warranty. And I'm 40% sure I damaged the PCB a tad when removing the card from the case. (Corner where the bracket for the PCIe cover is, my screwdriver was a bit thick and rubbed against it)

I sent the old card to them in the original box, and they were very adamant that they wouldn't give it back if I did send it. Not only did I get a warranty replacement, they actually sent back the original box I shipped my card in. The funniest part is that I know it's the original, because the serial number matched with the dead card, not the replacement card.

It sucks when you get conflicting moments. I'm sure 50% of those emails are fake, everyone loves to dog-pile on top of companies when a famous YouTuber calls them a scam, but My own experiences here in Canada do not reflect any of this, in fact... it's pretty much the total opposite...

Anyways. I hope Asus USA's stupid RMA disasters get fixed. Or that the Canadian branch can teach those guys a lesson in keeping customers happy over a bit of revenue that would be a rounding error for them...

I specifically avoided an ASUS board when building my new PC because of it! (I also went with a 12th gen Intel CPU rather than a 13th gen, but that was more out of cost, as the instability issues hadn't surfaced yet. Really dodged a bullet on that one!)
I am so glad I went with Gigabyte instead, because when I went to install an extra SSD a few months later, I accidentally gouged a critical trace on the board, and Gigabyte repaired my board free of charge!
It took a month and cost $30 in shipping, but it was a huge relief.
It wasn't perfect though; their support interface is pretty terrible! I signed up for no fewer than *three* separate accounts until I finally found the RMA page, and then completely missed the submit button for a week and only found it after sending an email...

I'm also thinking of grabbing a B580 (or maybe a B770 if it ever materializes) to replace my RX 5700 since 8GB VRAM is becoming an issue in bigger games lately.
